description.summary: The Flatwoods Monster is a 10-foot-tall, spade-headed entity allegedly encountered by a group of seven witnesses in Flatwoods, West Virginia, on the night of 12 September 1952, in connection with a fireball that crossed the eastern United States.
description.full: The Flatwoods Monster, also called the Braxton County Monster, is one of the most famous American UFO-related entity encounters of the 1950s. On the evening of 12 September 1952, a brilliant meteor was widely observed crossing the skies of Pennsylvania, Maryland, Ohio, and West Virginia. Around 7:15 PM, three boys in Flatwoods, West Virginia (Edward May, Fred May, and Tommy Hyer) saw what they took to be the object descending toward the property of farmer G. Bailey Fisher. Joined by Kathleen May (Edward and Fred's mother), 17-year-old West Virginia National Guardsman Eugene 'Gene' Lemon, and Neil Nunley and Ronnie Shaver, the group climbed Fisher's hill with a flashlight and Lemon's dog. Near the top they reported a pulsating glow, a foul mist that made them nauseous, and, in the beam of their light, a creature roughly 10 feet tall with a 'blood-red' face, glowing greenish-orange eyes, a spade-shaped head behind a black cowl, and clawed hands or appendages. The figure hissed, glided toward them, and the witnesses fled. The story was investigated locally by Sheriff Robert Carr, picked up by Charleston journalists, and given national circulation by Gray Barker in Fate magazine (January 1953) and by the early UFO community. The most-cited skeptical explanation, advanced in detail by Joe Nickell of the Committee for Skeptical Inquiry in 2000, identifies the entity as a barn owl perched in an oak tree, with the cowl and 'body' an artefact of the foliage and the witnesses' panic; the 'UFO' is widely accepted as a meteor that night, with a possible aircraft beacon contributing the pulsing red light. The case remains a foundational episode of West Virginia high-strangeness folklore and is now embodied in the Flatwoods Monster Museum in Sutton (opened 2018) and a series of giant monster-shaped chairs along the 'Braxxie Trail'.

etymology.origin: Named for the unincorporated community of Flatwoods in Braxton County, West Virginia, where the encounter occurred. 'Braxton County Monster' was the alternative name used in the early West Virginia press.
etymology.meaning: A locative cryptid name; 'Flatwoods' is the name of the village where the witnesses lived.
etymology.first_use: September 1952 in West Virginia regional press; 'Flatwoods Monster' became the standard name through the 1950s UFO literature.

features.description: Dark cowl-like head behind a red face described by Kathleen May as resembling 'the ace of spades'
Two windows or eye-like apertures emitting greenish-orange light
Witnesses described a metallic, pleated, skirt-like lower body rather than legs; the figure appeared to glide
Small clawed hands or short stub-like arms
Associated with the landed object, with intermittent red light interpreted by Nickell (2000) as plausibly an aircraft beacon
Sulfurous / metallic mist that the witnesses said caused nausea, watering eyes, and breathing difficulty

physical.morphology: Short-duration nighttime encounter with multiple witnesses. The 'monster' was seen briefly in a flashlight beam in dense woodland foliage; descriptions are consistent across the group on overall shape, colour, and the spade-head silhouette.

abilities.description: Witnesses reported the entity glided toward them rather than walked
Loud hiss heard immediately before the entity moved
Witnesses became nauseous and short of breath after the encounter; symptoms persisted for hours

habitat_preference: Adjacent to a glowing landed object
patterns: Associated with a meteor / fireball event widely observed across the eastern United States that evening

range.description: A single localized incident in central West Virginia. Subsequent regional folklore and tourism are concentrated in Braxton County and the town of Sutton.

first_recorded.source: Braxton Democrat (Sutton, WV) and Charleston Daily Mail, September 1952

peak_activity_periods.description: Primary press coverage from West Virginia papers through Gray Barker's January 1953 Fate magazine article

origins.cultural_roots: The Flatwoods incident occurred at the height of the 1950s American 'flying saucer' wave, three months after the high-profile July 1952 Washington, D.C. radar contacts. It became a foundational case in the early UFO literature and in the development of the 'high strangeness' close-encounter sub-genre.
origins.earliest_accounts: Eyewitness statements were taken by Braxton County Sheriff Robert Carr on the night of 12 September 1952 and reported in the Braxton Democrat and Charleston Daily Mail within days.
origins.folklore_connections: The Flatwoods Monster is paired in modern Appalachian folklore with the Mothman (Point Pleasant, 1966–67) and is part of the wider West Virginia high-strangeness tradition.

timeline.event: At c. 7:15 PM, a group of seven witnesses (Kathleen May, Edward May, Fred May, Tommy Hyer, Eugene Lemon, Neil Nunley, Ronnie Shaver) climb Fisher's hill in Flatwoods, WV and report encountering a 10-foot spade-headed entity by a glowing object
Sheriff Robert Carr, A. Lee Stewart Jr. of the Braxton Democrat, and others investigate the site, finding flattened grass, an oily substance, and an odor
Kathleen May and Eugene Lemon appear on the CBS television programme We the People, hosted by Dan Seymour
timeline.significance: First national television exposure of the case

timeline.event: Gray Barker publishes 'The Monster and the Saucer' in Fate magazine (January 1953)
Gray Barker expands the case in They Knew Too Much About Flying Saucers
timeline.significance: Anchors the case in 1950s UFO literature

timeline.event: Joe Nickell publishes a detailed skeptical investigation in Skeptical Inquirer identifying the entity as a barn owl in foliage
timeline.significance: Standard skeptical reference for the case

timeline.event: Flatwoods Monster Museum opens in Sutton, West Virginia, run by the Braxton County Convention and Visitors Bureau

history.modern_era: The case is sustained by ongoing tourism in Braxton County (the Flatwoods Monster Museum in Sutton, the giant chair 'Braxxie Trail', and the annual Flatwoods Monster Convention since 2019), by appearances in popular media including Bethesda's Fallout 76 (2018) and the History Channel's Project Blue Book (2019), and by continuing skeptical and folkloristic study.

notable.description: Following a brilliant meteor visible across the eastern United States, three boys saw what they thought was a craft descending into the Fisher property. They alerted Kathleen May and were joined by Eugene Lemon, Neil Nunley, and Ronnie Shaver. With a flashlight and Lemon's dog, the group climbed the hill. Near a glowing pulsating object, Lemon's flashlight beam fell on a 10-foot figure with a red, ace-of-spades-shaped face, glowing greenish-orange eyes, and a dark, skirted, metallic body. The entity hissed and glided toward them; the group fled, several reporting nausea and throat irritation.
evidence: Reported flattened grass and an oily skid mark on the hill (recorded by Sheriff Carr and reporter A. Lee Stewart Jr.)
Documented widely-witnessed meteor over the eastern US that night

factors: Multiple consistent witnesses across different ages and households
Same-day investigation by sheriff and journalist
No photographic or trace evidence preserved
Most-cited skeptical explanation (Nickell 2000) is the barn-owl hypothesis
credibility.notes: Foundational 1952 saucer-era case; widely cited and widely contested.

trace.name: Reported skid marks and oily residue on Fisher's hill
trace.description: Sheriff Robert Carr and Braxton Democrat reporter A. Lee Stewart Jr. reported flattened grass, a faint odor, and what they described as an oily skid mark on the hill the morning after the encounter.
trace.location: Fisher Farm hill, Flatwoods, West Virginia
trace.analysis: No physical sample preserved; later researchers (Nickell 2000) note alternative explanations including livestock paths.

documentary.name: 'The Monster and the Saucer'
documentary.description: Gray Barker's January 1953 Fate magazine article giving the case its first national circulation.
documentary.analysis: The single most influential early text on the case, though written from a pro-UFO perspective.

paranormal.name: Extraterrestrial close encounter
paranormal.description: Standard early UFO-literature reading: the witnesses encountered a landed extraterrestrial craft and an extraterrestrial entity wearing a suit.

scientific.name: Meteor + barn-owl misidentification
scientific.description: The descending object was a meteor (an event independently documented across the eastern US that night). The 'monster' was a startled barn owl perched in the lower branches of an oak above the witnesses, whose foliage formed the silhouette of a body and 'cowl'. Pulsing red light came from a nearby aircraft beacon. Nausea and throat irritation can be attributed to acute fear, the smell of burning ozone or aviation kerosene, and possibly local environmental factors.
evidence_cited: Documented red aircraft warning lights in the area
Ornithological behaviour of barn owls (Tyto alba) under flashlight illumination

skeptical.name: Mass panic and embellishment
skeptical.description: Skeptical commentators argue the witnesses, primed by extensive 1952 saucer coverage, encountered an ambiguous nocturnal stimulus (likely an owl) and constructed a coherent monster narrative collectively.
evidence_cited: 1952 was the peak year of the second great UFO wave
Witness ages (10–17, plus Kathleen May) and night-time conditions

traditions: West Virginia high-strangeness tradition (paired with Mothman)
stories: The 12 September 1952 encounter and Kathleen May's televised account on We the People (CBS, 1952)
folklore.beliefs: Locally treated as a defining piece of Braxton County identity, regardless of the believer/skeptic split, and curated through the Flatwoods Monster Museum and the Braxxie Trail.
